name: Credit card rewards value
title: Credit card rewards value: Formula, Example & Limits
description: Credit-card rewards are cash back, points, miles or similar benefits earned under a card program’s rules.
definition: Credit-card rewards are cash back, points, miles or similar benefits earned under a card program’s rules. Their usable value depends on eligible spending, earning rules, redemption choices, caps and fees.
explanation: Gross rewards differ from net value after annual charges and usable credits. A one-time welcome bonus belongs in a separate first-year illustration. Points require an explicit redemption-value assumption before they can be compared with cash amounts.
formula: Recurring net = annual gross reward value + usable net credits − annual fee; points value = points × cents per point / 100
formulaNote: Manual eligible-spending assumptions only. No issuer catalogue, live offer, automatic point valuation, approval or tax determination. Results are before unentered interest and other costs; all spending caps here are annual.

example.title: Separate $630 of cash back from the fee and one-time bonus
example.intro: Annual eligible spending: $12,000 at 3% and $18,000 at 1.5%; no category caps; $95 annual fee; $200 one-time bonus; no usable credits.
steps: Add the rewards, then subtract the $95 fee for recurring net value. Include the $200 bonus only in the first-year illustration.
example.answer: Gross annual cash back is $630; recurring net value is $535 and first-year value including the entered bonus is $735.
example.assumptions: Manual eligible-spending assumptions only. No issuer catalogue, live offer, automatic point valuation, approval or tax determination. Results are before unentered interest and other costs; all spending caps here are annual.

pitfall.title: Gross rewards are not the final economic benefit
pitfall.text: Deduct applicable recurring costs and evaluate card interest separately. Do not count restricted credits at face value unless they are actually usable.

tools.text: Separate recurring rewards, annual costs and a one-time bonus under your assumptions.
Account for borrowing interest and payoff timing separately from reward value.

name: Accounts receivable turnover
title: Accounts receivable turnover: Formula, Example & Limits
description: Accounts receivable turnover is period net credit sales divided by representative average trade receivables.
definition: Accounts receivable turnover is period net credit sales divided by representative average trade receivables. It expresses how many times that average balance turns over within the selected period.
explanation: Average-balance days sales outstanding converts the same relationship into days by dividing reporting-period days by turnover. Net credit sales, the receivables definition and the averaging interval must match.
formula: Turnover = net credit sales / average trade AR; average-balance DSO = reporting days × average AR / net credit sales
formulaNote: Matched-period net credit sales and trade receivables only. The two-point average may miss seasonality. DSO uses average balances here; no closing-balance, countback, aging, bad-debt or customer-credit analysis is provided.

example.title: Convert 12 annual receivables turns into about 30.42 collection days
example.intro: 365-day reporting period; $300,000 net credit sales; $25,000 representative average trade receivables.
steps: Divide net credit sales by average receivables: $300,000 / $25,000 = 12.
Divide 365 reporting days by turnover. Keep cash sales out of a credit-sales denominator.
example.answer: Turnover is 12 times for the year and average-balance DSO is about 30.42 days. This does not identify the age of any particular invoice.
example.assumptions: Matched-period net credit sales and trade receivables only. The two-point average may miss seasonality. DSO uses average balances here; no closing-balance, countback, aging, bad-debt or customer-credit analysis is provided.

pitfall.title: Collection days are not an invoice-aging report
pitfall.text: A single average can conceal overdue accounts, seasonality or changing customer terms. Use underlying records to investigate the reason for a ratio change.

tools.text: Translate matched credit sales and average receivables into turns and estimated collection days.
Inspect inventory turnover and holding days with a matching cost denominator.

name: Days payable outstanding
title: Days payable outstanding: Formula, Example & Limits
description: Days payable outstanding estimates the payment period represented by average trade payables relative to a matched-period purchases or cost flow.
definition: Days payable outstanding estimates the payment period represented by average trade payables relative to a matched-period purchases or cost flow. Its denominator convention is part of the definition.
explanation: A purchase-based calculation uses average payables divided by net credit purchases, multiplied by period days. Substituting cost of goods sold creates a proxy that can differ even with unchanged payables.
formula: Purchase-based DPO = reporting days × average trade AP / net credit purchases; proxy DPO explicitly substitutes COGS
formulaNote: Manual trade payables and matched credit purchases or a named COGS proxy. No inferred credit-purchase share, full inventory roll-forward, supplier aging, contract-term approval or cash-solvency decision.

example.title: Ten payables turns imply 36.5 payment days in a 365-day year
example.intro: $50,000 average trade payables; $500,000 same-period net credit purchases; 365 reporting days.
steps: DPO is $50,000 / $500,000 × 365. Match the trade-payables balance to the purchases financed by those suppliers.
example.answer: DPO is 36.5 days. Compare it with actual supplier terms and payment records before judging payment behavior.
example.assumptions: Manual trade payables and matched credit purchases or a named COGS proxy. No inferred credit-purchase share, full inventory roll-forward, supplier aging, contract-term approval or cash-solvency decision.

pitfall.title: A proxy change is not an operating improvement
pitfall.text: Label the denominator and keep it consistent across comparisons. A larger reported day figure alone does not establish favorable supplier terms or healthy liquidity.

tools.text: Compare explicitly labeled purchase-based and COGS-proxy payment-day estimates.
Inspect inventory turnover and holding days with a matching cost denominator.

scope: Manual trade payables and matched credit purchases or a named COGS proxy. No inferred credit-purchase share, full inventory roll-forward, supplier aging, contract-term approval or cash-solvency decision.

name: Cash conversion cycle
title: Cash conversion cycle: Formula, Example & Limits
description: The cash conversion cycle combines inventory holding days and customer collection days, then subtracts supplier-payment days.
definition: The cash conversion cycle combines inventory holding days and customer collection days, then subtracts supplier-payment days. It describes an operating cash-timing relationship under stated component definitions.
explanation: The operating cycle is inventory days plus collection days. CCC subtracts payables days from that total. All three components need compatible period and balance conventions before they are combined.
formula: CCC = DIO + DSO − DPO; operating cycle = DIO + DSO
formulaNote: Manual, matched-period balance ratios or supplied component days. Purchase-based and COGS-proxy payables are separate modes. This is not a cash-balance forecast, liquidity guarantee or supplier-payment instruction.

example.title: A 75-day operating cycle becomes a 15-day cash conversion cycle
example.intro: Inventory days 45; collection days 30; payables days 60; all entered on compatible definitions.
steps: Subtract payables days: 75 − 60. The operating cycle and cash conversion cycle are different measures.
example.answer: The cash conversion cycle is 15 days; the operating cycle is 75 days. Neither is a cash-balance forecast.
example.assumptions: Manual, matched-period balance ratios or supplied component days. Purchase-based and COGS-proxy payables are separate modes. This is not a cash-balance forecast, liquidity guarantee or supplier-payment instruction.

pitfall.title: A short or negative cycle is not a profit forecast
pitfall.text: The ratio does not establish cash reserves, invoice performance or the cost of maintaining supplier credit. Investigate the component changes behind the headline number.

tools.text: Combine inventory, collection and payment days with consistent definitions.
Inspect inventory turnover and holding days with a matching cost denominator.

name: Return on invested capital
title: Return on invested capital: Formula, Example & Limits
description: Return on invested capital compares annual after-tax operating profit with representative average invested capital.
definition: Return on invested capital compares annual after-tax operating profit with representative average invested capital. It connects an operating earnings numerator to a defined capital base.
explanation: NOPAT differs from net income after financing costs. A comparison with WACC subtracts rates in percentage points and relies on compatible capital and period assumptions; it is not a guaranteed investor return.
formula: ROIC = annual NOPAT / average invested capital; simplified economic profit = NOPAT − WACC × matching average capital
formulaNote: Annual manual operating-profit and invested-capital assumptions only. No live financial statements, balance-sheet reconstruction, intangible-capital adjustment or stock valuation. Loss tax benefits are not presumed unless explicitly selected.

example.title: Compare 12% ROIC with an entered 8% WACC
example.intro: Annual NOPAT $150,000; representative average invested capital $1,250,000; entered WACC 8%.
steps: Divide annual after-tax operating profit by average invested capital and express the ratio as a percentage.
Subtract the entered WACC in percentage points. On the same capital base, simplified economic profit is $150,000 − 8% × $1,250,000.
example.answer: ROIC is 12%, a 4-percentage-point spread over the assumed WACC; simplified annual economic profit is $50,000.
example.assumptions: Annual manual operating-profit and invested-capital assumptions only. No live financial statements, balance-sheet reconstruction, intangible-capital adjustment or stock valuation. Loss tax benefits are not presumed unless explicitly selected.

pitfall.title: Different capital definitions can produce different ROIC
pitfall.text: Keep operating scope and averaging conventions explicit. Comparing inconsistent numerators or borrowing a WACC from another capital definition can make the spread misleading.

tools.text: Compare after-tax operating profit with average invested capital and an entered WACC.
Compare period accounting earnings with average book equity.

name: Interest coverage ratio
title: Interest coverage ratio: Formula, Example & Limits
description: Interest coverage, or times interest earned, is EBIT divided by same-period interest expense.
definition: Interest coverage, or times interest earned, is EBIT divided by same-period interest expense. It relates accounting earnings before interest and income taxes to borrowing interest costs.
explanation: The denominator excludes principal repayments. A net-income bridge adds the signed income-tax amount and interest only when those amounts reconcile to the needed EBIT definition. DSCR uses a separately defined income and debt-service relationship.
formula: ICR / TIE = EBIT / interest expense; required EBIT = selected coverage target × same-period interest expense
formulaNote: Manual matched-period EBIT and borrowing-interest expenses, or a simple signed net-income/tax bridge. No EBITDA model, cash-flow forecast, lender approval, default probability or universal covenant threshold.

example.title: $100,000 EBIT covers $25,000 annual interest four times
example.intro: Same 12-month period: EBIT $100,000; borrowing interest expense $25,000; selected coverage target 3 times.
steps: Divide $100,000 by $25,000. EBIT is earnings before interest and income taxes; use an amount covering the same business and reporting period as interest.
At the selected target, required EBIT is 3 × $25,000 = $75,000. Compare that with actual EBIT to find $25,000 headroom.
Principal repayments, capital expenditure and working-capital cash needs are outside this interest-only denominator.
example.answer: Coverage is 4 times. The entered 3-times target is a comparison assumption, not a lending approval or a universal safety threshold.
example.assumptions: Manual matched-period EBIT and borrowing-interest expenses, or a simple signed net-income/tax bridge. No EBITDA model, cash-flow forecast, lender approval, default probability or universal covenant threshold.

pitfall.title: Interest coverage is not full debt-service coverage
pitfall.text: A high EBIT-to-interest multiple does not prove sufficient operating cash or funds for principal. Match the reporting period and the actual covenant definitions.

tools.text: Inspect EBIT-to-interest coverage and the earnings difference from a selected target.
Inspect a separately defined income-to-debt-service ratio, including the stated payment scope.

scope: Manual matched-period EBIT and borrowing-interest expenses, or a simple signed net-income/tax bridge. No EBITDA model, cash-flow forecast, lender approval, default probability or universal covenant threshold.
